intro: A global capital of theatre, museums, markets and music, where every neighbourhood feels like its own small city.
areas: Theatreland, Leicester Square, Chinatown and Soho’s late bars and restaurants.
Riverside walk past the London Eye, Southbank Centre, Tate Modern and Borough Market.
Street art, Brick Lane, Columbia Road flower market and East London’s club scene.
Camden Market, canal-side food stalls and a long history of live music.
sights: Free entry to world history, from the Rosetta Stone to the Parthenon sculptures.
Medieval fortress, Crown Jewels and the river’s most famous bridge.
Houses of Parliament, Big Ben’s Elizabeth Tower and Westminster Abbey.
Free collection of European paintings on the city’s best-known square.
Royal park walks, then the free V&A, Natural History and Science museums.
eat: London’s best-known food market, beside London Bridge.
Dim sum, noodles and bakeries on Gerrard Street.
Bagel bakeries, curry houses and the Sunday market.
A pub roast is a London weekend ritual; book ahead for popular spots.
night: Musicals and plays nightly; matinees are often cheaper.
Bars, cabaret, jazz at Ronnie Scott’s and LGBTQ+ venues.
Cocktail bars, late clubs and DJ nights in East London.
arrive: Heathrow (Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express), Gatwick (Gatwick Express or Thameslink), Stansted (Stansted Express), Luton (Luton DART plus train) and London City (DLR). Eurostar arrives at St Pancras.
around: The Tube, Elizabeth line, Overground, DLR and buses all take contactless; fares are capped daily and weekly. The Night Tube runs on some lines on Friday and Saturday nights.
pass: Use contactless or an Oyster card rather than paper tickets; daily capping does the work of a travel pass.
when: May–September for long light evenings and parks; December for Christmas lights and markets. It can rain any month.
tip: Stand on the right on Tube escalators, and touch in and out with the same card or phone to get the cap.

sources.title: Transport for London: fares and contactless

intro: A music, football and creative powerhouse with red-brick warehouses, big-name venues and a fierce independent streak.
areas: Independent shops, Afflecks, street art, record stores and late bars.
Restored mills and canal-side restaurants just north-east of the centre.
Department stores, riverside bars and the business district.
Canal basins, Roman fort remains and the Science and Industry Museum.
sights: Manchester’s industrial story on the site of the world’s oldest surviving passenger railway station.
John Rylands Research Institute and Library
Victorian Gothic reading room on Deansgate.
University museums with natural history, art and textiles.
Stadium tours at the homes of Manchester United and Manchester City.
eat: Food hall in a restored market building in the Northern Quarter.
Wilmslow Road in Rusholme, lined with South Asian and Middle Eastern restaurants.
One of the UK’s largest, centred on Faulkner Street.
Bakeries, pizza and modern British kitchens in former mills.
night: Cocktail bars, live music rooms and DJ bars.
One of the UK’s best-known LGBTQ+ nightlife quarters.
Co-op Live, AO Arena, O2 Apollo and Albert Hall for gigs.
arrive: Manchester Airport has direct trains to Piccadilly (around 15–20 minutes). Piccadilly and Victoria are the main rail stations.
around: Metrolink trams cover the centre and suburbs, and the free Bee Network buses and contactless capping make short trips simple. The centre is very walkable.
pass: Contactless tap-in on Metrolink caps fares across the day; a Bee Network day ticket also covers buses.
when: Spring to early autumn for terraces and festivals; winter for Christmas markets. Bring a waterproof any time.
tip: Football match days fill trams and pubs; check fixtures before you book a hotel.

sources.title: Bee Network / Transport for Greater Manchester

intro: A waterfront city of music, football and museums, where the Beatles story sits beside one of Britain’s friendliest nights out.
areas: Restored docks with museums, galleries and restaurants.
Independent cafés, vintage shops and global food.
Warehouse venues, food halls and creative studios.
Elegant terraces, both cathedrals and the Philharmonic.
sights: Museum at Royal Albert Dock about the band’s rise.
Museum of Liverpool & Merseyside Maritime Museum
Modern art at Royal Albert Dock (check the current reopening details).
Britain’s largest cathedral, with tower views.
Stadium tours at Liverpool FC’s Anfield and Everton’s new stadium at Bramley-Moore Dock.
eat: One of the city’s best streets for international cafés and restaurants.
Street-food hall in the Baltic Triangle.
Europe’s oldest Chinese community, marked by its grand arch.
night: Live music most days where the Beatles played.
Bars and clubs that stay busy late.
Warehouse clubs, live events and rooftop bars.
arrive: Liverpool John Lennon Airport is linked by bus to the city centre and Liverpool South Parkway station. Lime Street is the main rail station.
around: Merseyrail trains and buses cover the region; the centre is easy to walk. The Mersey Ferry crosses the river.
pass: Merseytravel day tickets cover trains, buses and the ferry; check current options before travel.
when: May–September for waterfront events; spring for the Grand National at Aintree.
tip: Bring ID for clubs and check the football fixtures, as match days transform the city.

intro: Scotland’s largest city: grand Victorian architecture, world-class free museums and a legendary live music scene.
areas: Restored warehouses with bars, restaurants and boutiques.
Kelvingrove, the University, Byres Road and Ashton Lane.
Argyle Street’s restaurant strip near the SEC venues.
Shawlands and Pollok Country Park with the Burrell Collection.
sights: Free museum with art, natural history and a daily organ recital.
Medieval cathedral and a Victorian hilltop cemetery with city views.
Free transport museum by the Clyde, with the Tall Ship Glenlee.
Art and antiquities in Pollok Country Park.
Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s legacy, also seen at The Lighthouse.
eat: Seafood, small plates and cocktail bars on Argyle Street.
Cobbled lane of pubs and restaurants in the West End.
Haggis, Cullen skink and a well-fired roll.
Weekend market in the East End.
night: Famous small venue on St Vincent Street.
A much-loved gig venue in the East End.
arrive: Glasgow Airport links to the centre by the airport express bus; Glasgow Prestwick has a rail link. Central and Queen Street are the main stations.
around: The Subway loops through the centre and West End; buses and trains cover the rest.
pass: Subway day tickets and SPT/ZoneCard options cover longer stays; check current fares.
when: May–September for long evenings; January for Celtic Connections music festival.
tip: Buy a ticket for a gig at the Barrowland or King Tut’s; the crowds are part of the show.

intro: Scotland’s capital packs a castle, a medieval Old Town and a Georgian New Town into one walkable, festival-loving city.
areas: Closes, wynds and historic buildings between the castle and Holyrood.
Georgian streets, Princes Street and George Street shops and bars.
Waterfront restaurants, bars and the Royal Yacht Britannia.
Village feel, independent shops and a Sunday market.
sights: On Castle Rock, home to the Honours of Scotland.
Hike Holyrood Park’s extinct volcano for views across the city.
Free museum with a rooftop terrace.
The monarch’s official residence in Scotland.
Monuments and one of the best sunset viewpoints.
eat: Seafood restaurants and bars around The Shore.
Pubs and restaurants beneath the castle.
Haggis, neeps and tatties, Cullen skink and shortbread.
night: Late bars and clubs in the Old Town.
Cocktail bars in grand Georgian buildings.
Sandy Bell’s is known for traditional sessions.
arrive: Edinburgh Airport is linked by tram and Airlink bus to the centre. Waverley is the main rail station with fast trains from London.
around: Lothian buses and the tram cover the city; the centre is compact but hilly.
pass: Lothian day tickets work on buses and the tram (airport journeys may cost more); contactless is accepted.
when: August for the Festival Fringe and International Festival (book well ahead); December for Hogmanay.
tip: Wear good shoes: the Old Town is steep and cobbled, and the weather changes fast.

intro: Britain’s second city, reborn around canals, Victorian landmarks and one of the country’s most diverse food scenes.
areas: Bullring, Grand Central and the Victorian civic squares.
Historic workshops, independent bars and restaurants.
Street art, warehouse venues, the Custard Factory and street food.
sights: Pre-Raphaelite collection; check current reopening details.
Striking modern library with rooftop gardens.
Birmingham has more miles of canal than Venice; walk the towpaths.
Explore the real streets and pubs linked to the era.
eat: Sparkbrook restaurants where the balti became famous.
Plenty of choice near New Street station.
night: Bars and clubs close to the canals.
Warehouse clubs, live music and the O2 Institute.
Utilita Arena and bp pulse LIVE for major tours.
arrive: Birmingham Airport has a rail station (Birmingham International) with fast trains to New Street. New Street, Moor Street and Snow Hill serve the centre.
around: West Midlands Metro trams link Snow Hill, New Street and Edgbaston; National Express West Midlands buses cover the region.
pass: Swift cards and contactless capping work on many buses and trams; check West Midlands Network for current options.
when: Spring to autumn for canals and terraces; December for the Frankfurt Christmas Market.
tip: Many sights are a short walk from New Street, so a central hotel saves on transport.

intro: Seaside, pier and pebble beach, with The Lanes, an LGBTQ+ heart and a big creative, music-loving spirit.
areas: Narrow historic alleys of jewellers, cafés and pubs.
Independent shops, vintage and street food.
The Palace Pier, i360, beach bars and arches.
Pride’s home, cafés and LGBTQ+ bars.
sights: Glass pod viewing tower on the seafront.
Chalk cliffs and downland a short bus ride away.
eat: Fish and chips on the beach
Vegan and vegetarian choice is excellent.
Bars and small kitchens under the promenade.
night: Clubs in the arches by the beach.
Concorde 2, Brighton Dome and many small venues.
arrive: Trains from London Victoria, London Bridge and Gatwick Airport arrive at Brighton station; Gatwick is about 30 minutes away.
around: Walk or cycle (BTN BikeShare); Brighton & Hove Buses run frequently, including nights.
pass: Brighton & Hove Buses offer day tickets and contactless capping; check the current fares.
when: May–September for the beach and the Brighton Festival and Fringe (May) and Pride (August).
tip: Pebble beaches: bring something soft to sit on and shoes for the water.

intro: Harbourside creativity, Banksy-era street art, Brunel engineering and one of the UK’s best club and sound-system scenes.
areas: Museums, bars and boats around the Floating Harbour.
Street art, independent shops and late venues.
Georgian terraces, the Suspension Bridge and the Downs.
St Nicholas Market and historic pubs.
sights: Brunel’s bridge over the Avon Gorge.
Brunel’s iron steamship in dry dock.
Free museum of Bristol life on the harbour.
Stokes Croft and Bedminster murals, including Upfest areas.
eat: Restaurants in shipping containers by the harbour.
One of the UK’s longest strips of independent shops and cafés.
night: Motion, Lakota and Thekla (a club on a boat).
Bars and venues that stay busy late.
Bars and boats for summer evenings.
arrive: Bristol Airport is linked to the city centre by an airport express bus. Bristol Temple Meads is the main station, with fast trains to London.
around: Walk the centre; buses (First and others) and ferries around the harbour do the rest.
pass: Bus day tickets and contactless are widely accepted; check current offers with the operators.
when: May–September for harbour festivals and outdoor events; Bristol Balloon Fiesta in August.
tip: Bristol is hilly; comfortable shoes help between Clifton and the harbour.

intro: Yorkshire’s big city: Victorian arcades, a strong music and student scene and easy days out in the Dales.
areas: Victoria Quarter arcades, Briggate and Trinity Leeds.
Student neighbourhoods, cricket and rugby grounds.
sights: National collection of arms and armour, free entry.
One of Europe’s largest covered markets.
Leeds Art Gallery & Henry Moore Institute
Huge park with lakes and gardens.
Cistercian abbey ruins in the suburbs.
eat: Food stalls and the market’s Food Hall.
The county’s signature, with a roast.
The city has a strong café scene.
night: Bars and DJ bars side by side.
Brudenell Social Club, O2 Academy and First Direct Arena.
Mint, Wire and others; check current line-ups.
arrive: Leeds Bradford Airport has a bus link to the centre. Leeds station is the main hub, with fast trains to London and across the north.
around: The centre is walkable; First and Arriva buses and local trains cover the region.
pass: West Yorkshire MCard day tickets cover buses (and rail options); check current products.
when: Spring to early autumn; summer brings Leeds Festival at Bramham Park in August.
tip: Use Leeds as a base for the Yorkshire Dales and York, both reachable by train.

intro: A proud, buzzing city on the Tyne with famous bridges, Grey Street grandeur and nights out to match.
areas: The Tyne bridges, bars and the Sunday market.
Grey Street’s elegant Georgian architecture and Grainger Market.
Creative valley with music venues and pubs.
BALTIC, The Glasshouse and the Millennium Bridge.
sights: Walk the Quayside past the Tyne Bridge and Gateshead Millennium Bridge.
Free art in a former flour mill.
The keep that gave the city its name.
Home of Newcastle United, with stadium tours.
eat: Historic indoor market with food stalls.
A local bread, best with ham and pease pudding.
Pubs and small kitchens in the valley.
night: The Cluny and other live music pubs.
arrive: Newcastle International Airport is on the Tyne and Wear Metro. Newcastle Central Station has fast trains to London and Edinburgh.
around: The Tyne and Wear Metro links the centre, airport, coast and Sunderland; buses cover the rest.
pass: Metro Day Tickets and Pop Pay As You Go cards cut costs; contactless is accepted.
when: Spring to autumn; the Great North Run in September.
tip: Ride the Metro to Tynemouth for the coast and a walk on Longsands.

intro: The Steel City: green hills, a compact centre, a celebrated music heritage and the Peak District on the doorstep.
areas: Peace Gardens, Winter Garden and the Millennium Gallery.
Former industrial area with breweries, bars and restaurants.
Bars and restaurants on the way to the Botanical Gardens.
sights: Sheffield’s industrial story, including a giant steam engine.
Large temperate glasshouse in the city centre.
National park less than half an hour away.
eat: Real-ale pubs, breweries and food halls.
A large food hall in Neepsend.
night: Traditional ale houses and modern bars.
arrive: Sheffield station has fast trains to London, Manchester and Leeds. The nearest airports are Manchester and Leeds Bradford.
around: Supertram lines and buses cover the city; the centre is walkable.
pass: Supertram day tickets and SYPTE options are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn for Peak District walks; June for Sheffield DocFest.
tip: Pack walking shoes: the Peak District begins at the city’s western edge.

intro: Robin Hood’s city: caves beneath the streets, historic pubs, two universities and a lively centre.
areas: Historic lace warehouses, bars and restaurants.
Independent shops, cafés and cocktail bars.
The city’s central square near the Council House.
sights: Castle grounds, gallery and Robin Hood story.
Underground caves beneath the Broadmarsh area.
One of the pubs claiming to be England’s oldest, partly cut into the castle rock.
Courtroom and prison history in the Lace Market.
eat: A local favourite, often with mint sauce.
night: Legendary live music and club venue.
arrive: East Midlands Airport has a Skylink bus to Nottingham. Nottingham station has direct trains to London St Pancras.
around: NET trams and frequent Nottingham City Transport buses cover the city.
pass: Robin Hood network day tickets cover trams and many buses; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn; Goose Fair in early October.
tip: Book ahead for cave tours, which run at set times.

intro: The Welsh capital: a castle in the city centre, a famous stadium, Victorian arcades and a revived bay.
areas: Cardiff Castle, St Mary Street and the arcades.
Wales Millennium Centre, the Senedd and waterfront restaurants.
Leafy streets, cafés and restaurants beside Bute Park.
Independent shops, bars and Roath Park lake.
sights: Roman walls, a Norman keep and Victorian interiors.
Tours of the home of Welsh rugby.
Free art and natural history museum.
St Fagans National Museum of History
Open-air museum of Welsh life, free entry.
eat: Victorian indoor market with Welsh cakes.
Traditional griddle cakes and a hearty stew.
Cafés and small restaurants in the Victorian arcades.
night: Bars and late-night food in the centre.
Clwb Ifor Bach and the Tramshed.
Rugby and gigs pack the city centre.
arrive: Cardiff Airport is linked by bus and by train from Rhoose station. Cardiff Central has fast trains to London Paddington.
around: The centre is compact; Cardiff Bus and local trains reach the Bay and suburbs.
pass: Cardiff Bus day tickets are available; check current fares.
when: Spring to autumn; Six Nations rugby weekends (February–March) are electric but busy.
tip: Hotels fill fast on match and concert days at the Principality Stadium.

intro: A city of shipbuilding history, murals and music, with a lively Cathedral Quarter and the Causeway Coast close by.
areas: Cobbled streets, pubs, live music and street art.
Titanic Belfast and the old shipyards.
Queen’s University, the Botanic Gardens and Ulster Museum.
City Hall, Victoria Square and St George’s Market.
sights: Exhibition where the RMS Titanic was built.
Free tours of the grand civic building.
Free museum in the Botanic Gardens.
Former Victorian prison with guided tours.
Political murals, best seen on a guided tour.
eat: Victorian market with food stalls at weekends.
A hearty breakfast with soda and potato bread.
Mashed potato with spring onion and butter.
night: Traditional music sessions and late bars.
The Duke of York & Kelly’s Cellars
The SSE Arena and Ulster Hall.
arrive: Belfast International (express bus) and George Best Belfast City (bus, minutes from the centre). Ferries arrive from Scotland and England.
around: Translink Metro buses and Glider rapid buses; the centre is walkable.
pass: Translink day tickets and contactless are available; check current fares.
when: May–September for long days and Causeway Coast trips.
tip: Take a black taxi tour for local stories behind the murals.

intro: Ireland’s capital: Georgian squares, literary history, the Liffey and pubs filled with music.
areas: Cobbled streets, pubs and traditional music.
Shopping and a lovely city park.
Modern waterfront and the EPIC museum.
Local pubs, cafés and the Jameson Distillery.
sights: Trinity College & the Book of Kells
Historic university and the illuminated manuscript.
The brewery experience with a rooftop bar.
Castle and a free museum of manuscripts and art.
Prison museum tied to Irish independence.
One of Europe’s largest city parks, with deer.
eat: Howth’s harbour is a DART ride away.
A hearty breakfast to start the day.
night: Busy and touristy, with music every night.
The Cobblestone in Smithfield is known for them.
arrive: Dublin Airport is linked by Airlink, Dublin Express and Aircoach buses. Heuston and Connolly are the main rail stations; ferries arrive at Dublin Port.
around: Luas trams, Dublin Bus and DART trains along the coast.
pass: Leap Card gives cheaper fares and daily caps; Leap Visitor Cards cover multiple days.
when: May–September for long evenings; St Patrick’s Day (17 March) is huge.
tip: Take the DART to Howth or Dún Laoghaire for cliff walks and seafood.
